arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Tayrani argued the Convention protects children from wrongful removal.
Mr. Joshi stated habitual residence asks where the child usually lives.
Mr. Pincus noted European courts consider the family and social environment.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case involves a two-year-old child removed from the United States. The lower court applied the Hague Convention to separate the child from her mother. the side that brought the case argues this application harms the child. the opposing side argues the Convention protects the child's home country.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to reject the requirement of parental agreement for habitual residence.
the opposing side wants the Court to uphold the lower court's finding of habitual residence.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues habitual residence is a flexible, fact-intensive concept that does not require parental agreement.
the opposing side argues habitual residence depends on the shared intent of the parents to reside in a country.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Alito asked if the agreement between parents is a pure question of fact.
Justice Ginsburg questioned the likelihood of parental agreement in acrimonious relationships.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines how courts determine a child's home country. It affects the rights of parents and children in international custody disputes. It clarifies the scope of the Hague Convention's protections.
